extracted.intended_audience: newspaper society-page writers and local theater reporters (newspaper staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for producing and editing newspaper society-page copy and local theater/movies reporting, covering space management, naming conventions, style, accuracy, picture arrangement, story structure, and the balance between reporting and criticism. Aimed at reporters and make-up/copy editors at local/regional newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit copy to allotted space
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept the 'dummy' space as unalterable and write copy to fit the inches allotted for the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have less copy than space, don't smuggle extra; if you have more copy than space, tell the make-up editor promptly so the page can be rescheduled or extra space provided. An early warning prevents last-minute flops (example: reporting 88 vs 124 inches available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify make-up editor promptly when overlength
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the make-up editor promptly if your copy will exceed the intended space so he can re-schedule pages or provide facing-page space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wait until late (e.g., noon) the facing page may already be prepared and the best that can be done is to flop the story far away. Early notice avoids the plight of a 'society flopover.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide make-up editor a checklist/list of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the make-up editor a list of your stories so he can check each one off as he fills the page and know none were missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a list, the editor may assume all society type has arrived and send the page; late stories can then be misplaced several pages away. A list lets him hunt successfully for any missing item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide enough headline-bearing stories
rubrics_metrics.description: For each column of space, prepare at least two stories that can carry headlines (unless chronicles are unusually long).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On dull days combine short personal mentions under a single lead (e.g., 'Among the families entertaining at dinner tonight will be...') to create items long enough for headlines and avoid a featureless, all-grey society page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust pictures to available space
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan photographs to fit the page layout and existing advertisements so the make-up editor can set them without trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid specifying picture combinations that clash with ads (e.g., two 2-column pictures side-by-side when an ad runs to the top). Such clashes force awkward placement and frustrate make-up editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary picture arrangements daily
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a variety of picture arrangements rather than always calling for the same layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample variations: three 2-column cuts under a six-column caption; two 2-column pictures under a four-column caption; three 1 1/3-column pictures under a four-column caption; two 1 1/3-column pictures with 1/3-column stories beside them; one 2-column picture flanked by one-column pictures. The idea: give the page a variety of structures and avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your news field and its relative importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as familiar with your beat (club, society groups) as other editors are with theirs; know which individuals and organizations are truly important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't, you'll underplay good news or overemphasize groups. Avoid stressing any one group too much to prevent jealousy; be aware that small clubs sometimes have excellent publicity and can generate more copy than you can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up advance notices with substantive coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not run advance stories and then fail to report the event afterwards in a substantial way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple tense change ('will talk' to 'talked') is lazy and unsatisfactory; add one or two sentences summarizing what was said to make the follow-up story substantial and satisfying to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid club-news bias based on personal affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let your own affiliations (alumna status, religion) lead you to overvalue certain clubs or to over-represent them in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some clubs may be resented for restrictive membership; too much stress on clubs affiliated with the writer's religion or background can cause trouble. Assess importance objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and verify names; don't rely on guesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify members' names rather than trusting publicity chairmen who may guess or spell names incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the city directory, telephone book, or club/program directories to check spellings and avoid errors that prompt readers to complain. Collect and keep club directories as reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize name identifications to avoid offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in how you identify people (titles, addresses) within a story to avoid appearing to slight or favor individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent identifications (e.g., calling one person by husband’s name and another by street address) can be perceived as insulting. Standardize forms of identification across the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in conventional, readable style rather than fanciful prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer conventional style on society pages; avoid overwrought or 'fancy' diction that readers may dislike and that can appear slushy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers 'play' with news and prefer conventional phrasing; attempt change slowly and consult copy-desk habits and house preferences. Overbidding for novelty can produce awkward, misleading phrasings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of platitudinous adjectives and unequal praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indiscriminately apply flattering adjectives (e.g., 'featured', 'charming') to some individuals and not others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either adorn everyone equally or avoid such ornaments; unequal use invites complaints of discrimination. Beware of creating a predictable set of descriptors that lose meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and follow the paper's house formulae/style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Study past editions and the style sheet to learn the newspaper's conventional forms for types of society stories (weddings, engagements) and other house habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some formulae are deliberate rules because readers prefer them; others are accidental habits. Proceed slowly in changing them; abrupt change can provoke charges of vanity and resistance from long-time staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe correct word usage and social terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise terms ('wedding' vs 'marriage', avoid saying a wedding 'occurred', don't say a clergyman 'performed' the service) and avoid culturally loaded words like 'lady' when inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'marriage' implies a ceremony; a 'wedding' is a social event. 'Performed' sounds acrobatic; 'rites' is funereal. Use terms consistent with readers' sensibilities; some papers prefer 'men and women' to 'ladies and gentlemen.' Be aware regional differences (e.g., 'debutante' age limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow engagement announcement convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the socially accepted phrasing for engagements: engagements are normally announced by the parents or guardians of the bride-elect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'Mr. and Mrs. Charles T. Denby announce the engagement of their daughter, Anita, to...' to avoid offending readers; social conventions change slowly, so follow prevailing local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write wedding stories for the bride and her parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the wedding story primarily as a record for the bride, her mother, and her father; the bride's name comes first and the bride is the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The groom is treated as stage property; the story should be composed as if to be clipped and pasted in the family Bible. Tailor content to local customs about pedigree and biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure wedding leads and paragraphs conventionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead: bride and groom names, time, place, clergyman; second paragraph: attendants; third: gowns (especially bride's); fourth: related events (reception, breakfast); next: honeymoon and 'at home' information; biography either after paragraph 3 or at end depending on local preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement of biography varies by city; follow local custom and the paper's file examples to determine preferred order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a 'wedding blank' to ensure accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and send a form listing all the information you'll need to the bride about two weeks before the wedding to ensure accuracy and to resolve disputes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a complaint about accuracy, the filled-in blank silences it. This reduces errors arising from last-minute confusion and misremembered details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include lists of names when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve and print lists of committee members, members of groups, and local names even when the substantive news is slight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists are valued by readers and build local goodwill. If space is tight, trim other copy (e.g., a speech) but keep name lists intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what readers value: 'who was there, what she wore, and names'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that society-page readers prize attendance and costume details and local name recognition above many other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect that information carefully; it is the 'recipe' for a society page that builds friendships for the newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write theater/movie reports as reporting first, criticism second
rubrics_metrics.description: For local audiences write primarily to report the show (description, useful guidance) rather than to offer highbrow dramatic criticism; criticism should be a small part (approximately 10%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for two reader groups: those who saw the performance and want to relive it, and those deciding whether to go. In most towns dramatic criticism in the New York high-culture mode is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: See the show twice and take professional notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend the performance twice: first to watch and enjoy, second to watch professionally and take notes for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes as if reporting a speech; the second viewing lets you analyze scenes and collect examples to explain why an audience laughed or why a scene worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not spoil plot enjoyment by reviewing the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid recounting the plot in your report because it spoils the pleasure for readers who will see the show and wearies those who have already seen it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on description, notable scenes, performances, and why they worked rather than summarizing the storyline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use four reporting devices in theater/movie pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ these procedures: (1) point out what others in the audience missed; (2) pick a central theme or impression and link the story to it; (3) give specific examples rather than vague praise; (4) compare with other pictures/productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: note understated technical elements (music, historical accuracy), unify copy around a recurring motif, cite specific scenes showing excellent photography, and contrast the show with comparable recent productions or performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be kindly, tolerant, and specific when criticizing amateurs
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing home-talent or little-theater performances, make allowances, be kindly and tolerant, and be specific in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid savage ridicule that alienates local performers. If you must criticize, explain concretely (show which scene or line failed) rather than using broad condemnations like 'total loss' or 'pitiful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make praise and criticism specific with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: State how a performer was 'superb' by describing the exact moments or techniques that showed it (e.g., 'her enthusiasm in the spelling-bee scene was the liveliest bit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics help readers who saw the performance recall the moment and help undecided readers know what to watch for; avoid vague superlatives without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include names of backstage and technical crew
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the 'behind the scenes' workers (cameramen, wardrobe custodians, carpenters) in your story; their work can materially affect the production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In home-grown shows the carpenters and painters may have created convincing atmosphere; include their names to recognize contributions and to inform readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a block structure for theater stories (Blocks 1–8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize theater stories into blocks: Block 1: the five Ws; Block 2: names of chief characters and roles (no comment unless specific); Block 3: names of secondary characters and roles; Block 4: explicit description of the show tied to a theme; Block 5: names of backstage crews; Block 6: names of chorus/battle-scene members; Block 7: names of musicians; Block 8: names of director, coach, publicity chairman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a usually minor group (e.g., battle-scene soldiers) has unexpected interest, elevate that block higher in the story. Follow this structure for clarity and to serve readers' needs.
